newsitem.title: GERMANY: Unemployment fuels strife between Bonn, labour.
newsitem.headline: Unemployment fuels strife between Bonn, labour.

text.p: German labour, government and business leaders moved further apart on Wednesday on ways to tackle growing unemployment even though all agreed the problem was heading toward dramatic proportions.

With unemployment already at a record 4.1 million workers and expected to edge up to 4.5 million this year, Chancellor Helmut Kohl and industry chiefs have shown interest in recent weeks in reviving a failed "Alliance for Jobs" with unions.
But a key labour leader has ruled out joining any new jobs roundtable discussions because Kohl pushed through tough labour reforms after the last round and employers were clamoring for more.

"I see no reason at the moment to resume the old round," said IG Metall chief Klaus Zwickel told the mass-circulation Bild newspaper. "Talks in the old form are senseless after our bitter experiences."
The refusal dampened chances for a revival of the alliance, which sought to halve unemployment by 2000, because it was Zwickel who helped found the effort early last year.
The effort collapsed last spring after Kohl's centre-right coalition pushed through an austerity package and laws allowing companies to cut sick pay and lay off workers more easily.
Kohl said last week that fighting unemployment was his number one priority. In his Bild interview, Zwickel said: "The situation is getting increasingly devastating."

Zwickel's hardened stance came a day after Hans Olaf Henkel, president of the Federation of German Industry, said Germany had already wasted a year in its effort to slash unemployment by the decade's end and urged more tax cuts to help companies create Meanwhile, the Free Democrats, junior partner in Kohl's coalition, said they would no longer seek further loosening of hire-and-fire laws or shop-opening hours -- two key reforms they had sought to stimulate hiring and economic growth.
This came as FDP member and Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt faced heavy criticism for saying that it is still too difficult to lay off workers in Germany's welfare state.
Opposition Social Democrats on Wednesday lashed out at Rexrodt and the coalition's labour and budget policies, saying they were responsible for the rise in joblessness.
"Their one-sided policy of budget-cutting has led to more and more unemployment," SPD fraction representative Anke Fuchs said in a parliamentary debate on unemployment.
"When an economics minister says it is still too hard to lay off people, a resignation is overdue," Fuchs said.
Labour Minister Norbert Bluem turned the blame back on the SPD for blocking other reforms that would reduce labour costs.
"You have prevented the new measures. You have blocked the labour reform law," he said. "You have that to answer for."
In the debate, Rexrodt insisted the solution still lies in cutting labour costs.
"We have to fight the causes of unemployment, and that is international competition and a labour cost structure that is not competitive," he said. "We have overregulated markets."
Rexrodt echoed the proposals outlined Tuesday night by German Labour Office president Bernhard Jagoda.
Jagoda suggested could create two million jobs by 2000 if wages were to rise no more than the inflation rate, and 40 percent of overtime hours were converted into new jobs.
He also said company contributions to social security and other programs would have to be reduced and government investments in job-creation programs increased.
